Below is a historically organized account of how “technical English in marketing” has evolved, spanning linguistic standardization, localization, globalization, and digitalization. Where possible, the narrative links milestones in marketing theory and communication practice to shifts in English usage and specialization.

1) From commodity markets to global brands: English as a business/marketing lingua franca (late 19th–mid 20th century)
- As markets expanded in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the need to distinguish goods and convey quality and origin spurred naming and brand practices that relied on legible labels and, increasingly, on English-derived terminology for export and multi-market communication. Historical reviews of “naming” describe how the convention crystallized in the late 19th century alongside mass consumerism and competition, with brand names often derived from founder surnames and evolving into strategic marketing assets as markets matured and competition intensified <cite id="d20f3723-1">The history of naming began with the development of production and increased competition. It was necessary to distinguish between different goods. In the past, companies have taken the names of their founders, whose last names guarantee a certain quality of the product. "The naming convention was built in the late 19th century, when the American consumer struggle was on a large scale."</cite>. 
- By the mid-20th century, “brand” itself had migrated into marketing discourse, where it denoted a trade/proprietary name and a set of consumer associations; this semantic integration anchored brand management in English as the medium of managerial and scholarly communication <cite id="d20f3723-2">According to Stern (2006), the term 'brand' entered marketing in 1922 as a compound expression and meant a trade or proprietary name. The term 'brand' was first found in the Germanic languages; to then expand into Old English… Moreover, the survival of brand is a signal of its vitality… Figure 1 provides a roadmap to the evolution of the 'brand' as a concept.</cite>. 
- Internationally, English emerged as the dominant lingua franca of business and marketing communication across geographies, enabling negotiation, contracting, and market entry among heterogeneous language communities. Contemporary syntheses note English’s hegemony in trade, diplomacy, telecommunications, and scientific publication, underpinning its centrality in marketing discourse; yet they also stress the need to manage multilingual capabilities alongside English proficiency for cross-border operations <cite id="6495f578-0">In international business, the dominant role of English as the lingua franca has been recognized by many authors… English is the language that is almost always used between an agent and an international company… English… is said to be the first global lingua franca and is the most widely used language in international trade, diplomacy, mass entertainment, international telecommunications and scientific publications… Nevertheless, a global marketplace suggests a need for skills in a multiplicity of languages.</cite> <cite id="6495f578-1">English, as the current global lingua franca, facilitates international communication… characterized by its adaptability and efficiency, often leading to the development of simplified forms… Business English… encompasses… conventions, jargon, and idiomatic expressions unique to the business world… intersects with English for Specific Purposes (ESP).</cite>. 
- Practically, English became indispensable in marketing channels and managerial interfaces. Case-based work from emerging economies shows entrepreneurs treating English as a marketing tool to access global markets, even while acknowledging difficulties; this underscores English’s instrumental role in import–export, tourism, and hospitality, and indicates that functional communicative competence is often valued over formal grammaticality in transactional marketing contexts <cite id="6495f578-2">Indonesian online businessmen mainly use English as a marketing tool… despite the difficulties they face… they rely on it for various business endeavors.</cite> <cite id="6495f578-3">Members and employees in company networks and partnerships had to be able to use ELF professionally… English has widened as day-to-day communication.</cite> <cite id="6495f578-4">English significantly influences import and export marketing… For marketing and business purposes, it is not necessary to use standard or correct English.</cite>.

2) Technical/managerial lexicon and terminology: glossaries, dictionaries, and branding jargon (mid–late 20th century)
- Marketing lexicons and glossaries codified technical English for brand management, advertising, and retailing, reflecting the shift from artisanal to mass-market economies. Comparative studies of brand naming in English highlight phonosemantic and psychoanalytic tools, and document how research-based methods supplanted intuitive, descriptive naming—marking the emergence of a practical, academic apparatus for “naming” as a discipline in marketing <cite id="d20f3723-1">We see in scientific sources that the term naming is defined differently… The Encyclopaedia of Marketing explains the term naming as follows: "Naming… the process of creating company and brand names based on the use of phonosemantic and psychoanalysis tools of linguistics."… With the development of market relations… "naming" has become an integral part of marketing… a practical academic approach to the selection of names has begun. Naming has become a discipline.</cite>. 
- Branding research consolidated key marketing English constructs such as “positioning,” “unique selling proposition (USP),” and “identity,” embedding them in managerial jargon and academic discourse. Surveys of branding’s entry into marketing show how the brand evolved from a proprietary name into a multidimensional construct governed by managers, media, consumers, and technology, formalizing a specialized lexicon that travels globally via English <cite id="d20f3723-2">Bastos and Levy… explain it as: …the evolution of the brand from a simple entity… to the brand as a complex entity that is multi-dimensional and multi-functional… The term 'brand' entered marketing in 1922 as a trade or proprietary name.</cite>. 
- Linguistic research on brand names in English expanded from phonetics and morphology to cross-modal symbolism and sound–meaning mappings, systematizing how English phonology contributes to brand recall and differentiation; this represents the professionalization of “technical English” in marketing communication through empirical study and codified principles <cite id="d20f3723-0">Initial marketing studies… examined… number of syllable, singular or plural forms and hard or soft sounding words in English… with… phonetic, orthographic, morphologic and semantic characteristics of top 200 US brand names for the years 1971 to 1985… The interest towards linguistic characteristics… and sound qualities… of US brand names originating from English have continued in 2000s.</cite> <cite id="d20f3723-3">The first marketing study on sound symbolism readily accessible was published in 1972… since 1970, 46 marketing studies on sound symbolism… effects… have been dominantly verified for English.</cite>. 
- Pedagogically and professionally, “marketing English” developed as an ESP area emphasizing clarity, precision, and business jargon, distinct from general English; this reflects the need for specialized communicative competencies in advertising, sales, and corporate marketing, often prioritizing functional over formal accuracy <cite id="6495f578-1">Business English… conventions, jargon, and idiomatic expressions unique to the business world… intersects with ESP… characterized by clarity, precision, and formality.</cite> <cite id="6495f578-4">Marketing and business purposes… it is not necessary to use standard or correct English.</cite> <cite id="6495f578-4">Marketing language… operates under less strict linguistic rules compared to specialized terminology (which should undergo standardization procedures)… flexibility has given rise to a lively and diverse linguistic landscape within the marketing domain.</cite>.

3) Globalization, localization, and transcreation (1980s–2000s)
- As multinational corporations expanded post-WWII, English became the internal and external lingua franca, but effective marketing required adaptation to local cultures and languages. Management studies identify English as the common language adopted in multinationals even where few spoke it natively, while simultaneously noting the persistent importance of multilingual fluency for negotiation and customer relations <cite id="6495f578-0">The English language has… such a strong position in multinational companies that it can be adopted as the common language in a company where no one actually speaks English as their mother tongue… Yet most have fluency… English does not always work without other languages.</cite>. 
- Marketing translation moved beyond literal equivalence toward communicative and aesthetic equivalence, with “domestication” and “foreignization” as core strategies and “transcreation” emerging as a creative, culturally attuned process to preserve intent, tone, and impact across markets. Comparative slogan translation studies demonstrate how English-targeted adaptations must align with target-audience values, clarity, and rhythm to achieve persuasive equivalence, often reading as “natively crafted” for the local context <cite id="754e6e9c-1">A domestication-oriented approach, strategically combined with transcreation and addition, yields optimal communicative outcomes… translation evaluation… across… value compatibility, communicative effectiveness, and aesthetic-emotional appeal… translations… as if originally crafted for the specific cultural context; functional equivalence with the original commercial persuasive intent.</cite> <cite id="754e6e9c-3">Transcreation… refers to the adaptive process of recreating a message in another language while preserving its intent, tone, and impact… beyond linguistic transfer to incorporate cultural nuance, humor, idioms, and local trends.</cite> <cite id="754e6e9c-4">In the global consumer market, brand translation is no longer a simple language conversion issue but an important issue involving cultural adaptation and market strategy… a balanced use of domestication and foreignization… effectively bridging cultural differences while preserving the brand's heritage.</cite>. 
- English thus functions as a control language for global campaigns while local languages and English-derived variants circulate in adapted slogans, packaging, and media. Research on advertisement slogans underscores that transcreation integrates deep brand understanding, cultural empathy, and creativity to trigger emotional resonance—capabilities that are central to technical English in marketing as it crosses markets <cite id="754e6e9c-0">Transcreation… emphasizes its uniqueness in the traditional translation paradigm… four key steps… understanding of the brand essence, sensitive response to cultural differences, flexible use of language skills, and incorporation of creative elements… impact on cultural exchange, brand communication and translation field, particularly in the era of globalization.</cite> <cite id="754e6e9c-3">Transcreation acknowledges that effective communication in commercial contexts requires not just linguistic skill, but also marketing insight and cultural empathy.</cite>. 
- Corporate language strategies reflect these dual imperatives: English proficiency as a baseline for global coordination, yet investment in multilingual and cross-cultural competencies to avoid failure or offense in local markets <cite id="6495f578-0">One priority for companies is to ensure they have a high-level capability in English… English remains as important as ever on the Internet, other languages… becoming comparatively more important.</cite> <cite id="6495f578-1">Business English… requires an understanding of the cultural and contextual nuances that influence business interactions… intersects with ESP.</cite>.

4) Digital-era technical English: SEO, social media, data, and analytics (2000s–present)
- The internet and social platforms accelerated the need for technically precise yet accessible English in marketing. English remains the primary vehicle for global commerce and digital interfaces, while non-English languages grow in relative importance; this hybrid landscape drives English to be optimized for search engines, platform algorithms, and cross-lingual virality, while local content strategies deploy adapted terminology and style <cite id="6495f578-0">While English remains as important as ever on the Internet, other languages such as Chinese, Russian, Spanish and Portuguese are becoming comparatively more important.</cite>. 
- Marketing English absorbed technical vocabulary from data and digital domains—keywords, meta tags, engagement metrics, targeting, conversion, A/B testing—shaping SEO-optimized content and analytics-driven messaging. Studies of linguistic adaptation emphasize that marketing language departs from strict grammaticality to prioritize functional clarity and platform affordances, creating a flexible, hybrid linguistic landscape that is both a subject of academic inquiry and pedagogical resource <cite id="6495f578-4">Marketing language… operates under less strict linguistic rules compared to specialized terminology… giving rise to a lively and diverse linguistic landscape within the marketing domain, presenting an intriguing sphere for scientific research, and valuable language teaching resource.</cite>. 
- Cross-border digital campaigns continue to rely on transcreation workflows between English source materials and localized outputs, with intercultural evaluation criteria aligned to audience values, clarity, and emotional rhythm; this underscores how “technical English” is not merely standardized grammar but a set of communicative techniques adapted to market semantics and media environments <cite id="754e6e9c-1">Systematic assessment across… value compatibility, communicative effectiveness, and aesthetic-emotional appeal… translations… functionally equivalent with the original commercial persuasive intent.</cite> <cite id="754e6e9c-3">Transcreation… preserves intent, tone, and impact… incorporates cultural nuance, humor, idioms, and local trends.</cite>. 
- Emerging AI tools are now integrated into transcreation pipelines, challenging professional education and practice by enabling rapid generation and prompting-based customization. Comparative evaluations show that targeted AI training can raise student transcreation quality to surpass professionals on some metrics, while emphasizing the irreplaceable role of human judgment in strategy, creativity, and ethical adaptation—further professionalizing and technologizing “technical English” in marketing <cite id="754e6e9c-2">Traditional translation methods often fail to capture brand-specific emotional resonance… AI tools may address this challenge… students surpassed professionals, as judged by expert raters… underscores the value of human judgment in crafting prompts and choosing optimal AI outputs.</cite>.

5) Professionalization and education: English for Marketing (EFM) and ESP (mid–late 20th–21st century)
- English for Marketing emerged as a subfield of ESP to train communicative competencies in advertising, brand management, retail, and corporate marketing, integrating terminology, cross-cultural rhetoric, and digital tools. Studies emphasize that marketing English prioritizes clarity, persuasion, and contextual appropriateness over strict standardization, aligning with real-world practices where functional accuracy and audience tuning dominate <cite id="6495f578-1">Business English… clarity, precision, and formality… requires… cultural and contextual nuances… intersects with ESP.</cite> <cite id="6495f578-4">Marketing language… operates under less strict linguistic rules compared to specialized terminology… flexibility has given rise to a lively and diverse linguistic landscape… valuable language teaching resource.</cite>.

6) Power, inequality, and contested norms in “global English” for marketing
- Historical syntheses warn that English as a lingua franca carries cultural and economic power, shaping global business norms and practices; reliance on English in marketing can privilege certain standards while marginalizing others, reinforcing the need for multilingual strategies and equitable localization practices <cite id="6495f578-1">English… carries cultural and economic power, influencing global business practices and norms… crucial in understanding how English facilitates economic transactions… and challenges for those less proficient.</cite>. 
- In practice, many marketers adopt simplified or adapted varieties of English to ensure clarity across heterogeneous audiences, sometimes favoring transliteration, calquing, or phonosemantic adaptation (as in Coca-Cola’s Chinese transcreation) to bridge gaps—illustrating how “technical English” is contested, hybridized, and continuously re-engineered for market success <cite id="754e6e9c-3">Transcreation… acknowledges… cultural empathy… classic example… Coca-Cola… phonetic and semantic adaptation… enhances brand appeal.</cite> <cite id="d20f3723-1">Marketing… naming… uses phonosemantic and psychoanalytic tools… naming has become a discipline.</cite>.

- Late 19th–early 20th century: Branding and naming professionalize; English becomes the medium of managerial and scholarly brand discourse; marketing English codifies jargon and conventions for competitive differentiation <cite id="d20f3723-2">The term 'brand' entered marketing in 1922 as a trade or proprietary name… evolution of the brand into a complex, multidimensional entity.</cite> <cite id="d20f3723-1">The naming convention was built in the late 19th century… naming has become an integral part of marketing… a practical academic approach has begun.</cite>.

Title: Sound Symbolism in Marketing: An Integrative Review of Marketing Studies into Sound Symbolism
Snippet: This study is designed as a review study which addresses the literature studying sound symbolism with respect to brand naming. Other marketing studies that addressed sound symbolism in terms of cross-modal correspondences are out of the scope of this study because sounds in cross modal correspondences are not limited with speech sounds by which the brand names are created (e.g., Crisinel and Spence, 2009;Simner et al., 2010). The investigation involves the research published in English in marketing literature between 1970 and 2019 because the first marketing study on sound symbolism, which is readily accessible, was published in 1972 by Peterson and Ross. Additionally, the sound symbolism effects in brand naming have been dominantly verified for English (e.g., Klink, 2000;2001;2003;Lowrey and Shrum, 2007;Yorkston and Menon, 2004). Since this study attempts to draw a comprehensive map for the effects of sound symbolism in marketing, articles included in the study were limited according to the following criteria: (a) only marketing research on sound symbolism was examined; (b) since there is an extensive literature on sound symbolism, articles only appeared in marketing related publications were included; (c) articles only published in academic journals that readily accessible were used; and (e) only empirical marketing research based on primary and/or secondary data were included into the study and so conceptual and case studies were excluded from the review process. 

In order to identify pertinent marketing studies, electronic databases; Ebsco, Elsevier, Emerald, Jstor, Sage Journals, Science Direct, Springer Link, Taylor & Francis Online Journals, and Wiley Online Library were searched with the keywords "sound symbolism", "phonetic symbolism", "phonetic iconicity" phonetic symbolism"; "onomatopoeia"; "phonaesthesia"; "phonetic motivation"; and "synesthesia" in combination with "marketing", "brand", "branding", and "brand name". Title: AI-Powered Transcreation in Global Marketing: Insights from Iran
Snippet: This study examines AI-powered transcreation’s role in improving cross-cultural brand communication. We employed GPT-3 to evaluate AI’s ability to enhance global marketing through improved translation and adaptation of brand messages. Traditional translation methods often fail to capture brand-specific emotional resonance across cultures, but AI tools may address this challenge. Our research compared 10 translation students and 10 professional translators in translating/transcreating brand taglines from Persian to English. Title: Sound Symbolism in Marketing: An Integrative Review of Marketing Studies into Sound Symbolism
Snippet: Initial marketing studies on sound symbolism were the ones which examined the use of linguistic approach with respect to number of syllable, singular or plural forms and hard or soft sounding words in English (Peterson and Ross, 1972); with respect to phonetic, orthographic, morphologic and semantic characteristics of top 200 US brand names for the years 1971 to 1985 (Vanden Bergh et al., 1987) and sound qualities with respect to initial sounds of US brand names for the years 1972 to 1979 (Schloss 1981;Vanden Bergh et al., 1990). On the basis of these initial sound-related marketing studies, it is very difficult to state that sound symbolism has been conceptualized properly. Nevertheless, these studies have furthered the sound symbolic marketing studies. The interest towards linguistic characteristics (Arora et al., 2015;Lowrey et al., 2003) and sound qualities (Doorn et al., 2016;Pogacar et al., 2015) of US brand names originating from English have continued in 2000s. Title: National and Cultural Features of Creating a Name (Naming) in the Language

Title: Sound Symbolism in Marketing: An Integrative Review of Marketing Studies into Sound Symbolism
Snippet: This study is designed as a review study which addresses the literature studying sound symbolism with respect to brand naming. Other marketing studies that addressed sound symbolism in terms of cross-modal correspondences are out of the scope of this study because sounds in cross modal correspondences are not limited with speech sounds by which the brand names are created (e.g., Crisinel and Spence, 2009;Simner et al., 2010). The investigation involves the research published in English in marketing literature between 1970 and 2019 because the first marketing study on sound symbolism, which is readily accessible, was published in 1972 by Peterson and Ross. Additionally, the sound symbolism effects in brand naming have been dominantly verified for English (e.g., Klink, 2000;2001;2003;Lowrey and Shrum, 2007;Yorkston and Menon, 2004). Since this study attempts to draw a comprehensive map for the effects of sound symbolism in marketing, articles included in the study were limited according to the following criteria: (a) only marketing research on sound symbolism was examined; (b) since there is an extensive literature on sound symbolism, articles only appeared in marketing related publications were included; (c) articles only published in academic journals that readily accessible were used; and (e) only empirical marketing research based on primary and/or secondary data were included into the study and so conceptual and case studies were excluded from the review process. 

In order to identify pertinent marketing studies, electronic databases; Ebsco, Elsevier, Emerald, Jstor, Sage Journals, Science Direct, Springer Link, Taylor & Francis Online Journals, and Wiley Online Library were searched with the keywords "sound symbolism", "phonetic symbolism", "phonetic iconicity" phonetic symbolism"; "onomatopoeia"; "phonaesthesia"; "phonetic motivation"; and "synesthesia" in combination with "marketing", "brand", "branding", and "brand name". Additionally, references of relevant articles were also scanned manually to identify other relevant marketing studies. In total, 46 marketing studies on sound symbolism published in 17 different sources fulfilled the criteria for being included into the review (see Appendix A).

This study is designed as a review study which addresses the literature studying sound symbolism with respect to brand naming. Other marketing studies that addressed sound symbolism in terms of cross-modal correspondences are out of the scope of this study because sounds in cross modal correspondences are not limited with speech sounds by which the brand names are created (e.g., Crisinel and Spence, 2009;Simner et al., 2010). The investigation involves the research published in English in marketing literature between 1970 and 2019 because the first marketing study on sound symbolism, which is readily accessible, was published in 1972 by Peterson and Ross. Additionally, the sound symbolism effects in brand naming have been dominantly verified for English (e.g., Klink, 2000;2001;2003;Lowrey and Shrum, 2007;Yorkston and Menon, 2004). Since this study attempts to draw a comprehensive map for the effects of sound symbolism in marketing, articles included in the study were limited according to the following criteria: (a) only marketing research on sound symbolism was examined; (b) since there is an extensive literature on sound symbolism, articles only appeared in marketing related publications were included; (c) articles only published in academic journals that readily accessible were used; and (e) only empirical marketing research based on primary and/or secondary data were included into the study and so conceptual and case studies were excluded from the review process. 

In order to identify pertinent marketing studies, electronic databases; Ebsco, Elsevier, Emerald, Jstor, Sage Journals, Science Direct, Springer Link, Taylor & Francis Online Journals, and Wiley Online Library were searched with the keywords "sound symbolism", "phonetic symbolism", "phonetic iconicity" phonetic symbolism"; "onomatopoeia"; "phonaesthesia"; "phonetic motivation"; and "synesthesia" in combination with "marketing", "brand", "branding", and "brand name". Additionally, references of relevant articles were also scanned manually to identify other relevant marketing studies. In total, 46 marketing studies on sound symbolism published in 17 different sources fulfilled the criteria for being included into the review (see Appendix A).

Title: Transcreation in Advertisement Slogans from the Perspective of Communicative Translation Theory
Snippet: Through in-depth analysis of advertisement slogans, the present study probes into the unique contribution of trancreation in conveying brand messages and triggering emotional resonance of the audience. The study firstly outlines theoretical basis of transcreation from the perspective of Communicative Translation Theory, emphasizing its uniqueness in the traditional translation paradigm. Then the four key steps of transcreation, including in-depth understanding of the brand essence, sensitive response to cultural differences, flexible use of language skills, and incorporation of creative elements, are examined by means of case analysis in advertisement translation. Finally, the article sums up the positive impact of transcreation on cultural exchange, brand communication and translation field, particularly in the era of globalisation.

Title: A Study on English Translation of Chinese Brand Slogans in Global Campaigns from an Intercultural Communication Perspective
Snippet: For mass consumer markets, a domestication-oriented approach, strategically combined with transcreation and addition, yields optimal communicative outcomes. 

Finally, regarding translation evaluation, this study proposes a systematic assessment across three intercultural dimensions: value compatibility, which examines whether the translated value proposition aligns with the target cultural dimensions; communicative effectiveness, referring to the clarity of brand message delivery and adherence to low-context expression norms; and aesthetic-emotional appeal, concerning the translation's phonological rhythm and emotional impact to resonate with the target audience. Successful translations are generally characterized by target-audience-centricity, reading as if originally crafted for the specific cultural context; functional equivalence with the original commercial persuasive intent; and global sublimation of brand value, whereby regionally specific cultural features are transformed into universal emotional propositions. 

The English translation of Chinese brand advertising slogans constitutes a complex process of cross-cultural reconstruction. Its ultimate success hinges on whether translators can be guided by intercultural communication theory and flexibly employ strategies such as domestication and transcreation to produce translations that seamlessly align with the target audience in terms of values, communicative function, and aesthetic appeal. This process demands that translators evolve from passive linguistic artisans into proactive intercultural communication experts and co-creators of brand value, thereby effectively enhancing the soft power of Chinese brands in global communication.

Title: AI-Powered Transcreation in Global Marketing: Insights from Iran
Snippet: This study examines AI-powered transcreation’s role in improving cross-cultural brand communication. We employed GPT-3 to evaluate AI’s ability to enhance global marketing through improved translation and adaptation of brand messages. Traditional translation methods often fail to capture brand-specific emotional resonance across cultures, but AI tools may address this challenge. Our research compared 10 translation students and 10 professional translators in translating/transcreating brand taglines from Persian to English. An initial test without AI showed professionals outperforming students. After six weeks of GPT-3 training, however, students surpassed professionals, as judged by expert raters using standardized criteria. The findings indicate that targeted AI training can improve transcreation quality. The study also underscores the value of human judgment in crafting prompts and choosing optimal AI outputs. These results also offer insights for translation education, professional training, and global marketing strategies.

Title: Transcreating Persuasion: A Functionalist Approach to Slogan Translation in Global Fashion Advertising
Snippet: Transcreation-a portmanteau of translation and creation-refers to the adaptive process of recreating a message in another language while preserving its intent, tone, and impact. Often used in advertising and branding, transcreation goes beyond linguistic transfer to incorporate cultural nuance, humor, idioms, and local trends. This approach is especially critical in markets where literal translations may fail to resonate or even cause offense. For instance, the Chinese translation of Coca-Cola as "可口可乐" (meaning "tasty and fun") is a classic example of transcreation that enhances brand appeal through phonetic and semantic adaptation. Transcreation acknowledges that effective communication in commercial contexts requires not just linguistic skill, but also marketing insight and cultural empathy.

Title: Study on the Translation of Chinese Chic Brands from the Perspective of Domestication and Foreignization: A Case Study of CHAGEE
Snippet: In the context of globalization, cultural exchange continues to deepen and brands and culture are gradually integrating. With its unique cultural connotation and design aesthetics, Chinese chic brands began to appear on the world stage. These brands not only represent China's cultural confidence but also reflect the thriving development of China's creative industry. However, the dissemination and acceptance of a brand largely rely on effective cross-cultural communication. The selection of translation strategies in cross-cultural communication is crucial. As two main translation strategies, domestication and foreignization have different guiding principles in translating brand names, slogans and cultural attributes. This paper focuses on CHAGEE, a Chinese chic brand and discusses how domestication and foreignization strategies can better convey the core values and cultural characteristics of the brand in the cross-cultural context. As a typical emerging chic brand in China, CHAGEE provides us with a good example for observing and analyzing the practical application of these two translation strategies in international market positioning and communication. 

In the global consumer market, brand translation is no longer a simple language conversion issue but an important issue involving cultural adaptation and market strategy. Through this study, we aim to provide valuable insights for translation practitioners, brand managers, and cross-cultural communication researchers and contribute to the international dissemination of Chinese culture. This article argues that CHAGEE's successful expansion in the international market is largely due to its balanced use of domestication and foreignization translation strategies, effectively bridging cultural differences while preserving the brand's Chinese tea culture heritage.

The English translation of Chinese brand advertising slogans constitutes a complex process of cross-cultural reconstruction. Its ultimate success hinges on whether translators can be guided by intercultural communication theory and flexibly employ strategies such as domestication and transcreation to produce translations that seamlessly align with the target audience in terms of values, communicative function, and aesthetic appeal. This process demands that translators evolve from passive linguistic artisans into proactive intercultural communication experts and co-creators of brand value, thereby effectively enhancing the soft power of Chinese brands in global communication.

documents.title: AI-Powered Transcreation in Global Marketing: Insights from Iran
documents.snippet: This study examines AI-powered transcreation’s role in improving cross-cultural brand communication. We employed GPT-3 to evaluate AI’s ability to enhance global marketing through improved translation and adaptation of brand messages. Traditional translation methods often fail to capture brand-specific emotional resonance across cultures, but AI tools may address this challenge. Our research compared 10 translation students and 10 professional translators in translating/transcreating brand taglines from Persian to English. An initial test without AI showed professionals outperforming students. After six weeks of GPT-3 training, however, students surpassed professionals, as judged by expert raters using standardized criteria. The findings indicate that targeted AI training can improve transcreation quality. The study also underscores the value of human judgment in crafting prompts and choosing optimal AI outputs. These results also offer insights for translation education, professional training, and global marketing strategies.

documents.title: Transcreating Persuasion: A Functionalist Approach to Slogan Translation in Global Fashion Advertising
documents.snippet: Transcreation-a portmanteau of translation and creation-refers to the adaptive process of recreating a message in another language while preserving its intent, tone, and impact. Often used in advertising and branding, transcreation goes beyond linguistic transfer to incorporate cultural nuance, humor, idioms, and local trends. This approach is especially critical in markets where literal translations may fail to resonate or even cause offense. For instance, the Chinese translation of Coca-Cola as "可口可乐" (meaning "tasty and fun") is a classic example of transcreation that enhances brand appeal through phonetic and semantic adaptation. Transcreation acknowledges that effective communication in commercial contexts requires not just linguistic skill, but also marketing insight and cultural empathy.

documents.snippet:
In the context of globalization, cultural exchange continues to deepen and brands and culture are gradually integrating. With its unique cultural connotation and design aesthetics, Chinese chic brands began to appear on the world stage. These brands not only represent China's cultural confidence but also reflect the thriving development of China's creative industry. However, the dissemination and acceptance of a brand largely rely on effective cross-cultural communication. The selection of translation strategies in cross-cultural communication is crucial. As two main translation strategies, domestication and foreignization have different guiding principles in translating brand names, slogans and cultural attributes. This paper focuses on CHAGEE, a Chinese chic brand and discusses how domestication and foreignization strategies can better convey the core values and cultural characteristics of the brand in the cross-cultural context. As a typical emerging chic brand in China, CHAGEE provides us with a good example for observing and analyzing the practical application of these two translation strategies in international market positioning and communication. 

In the global consumer market, brand translation is no longer a simple language conversion issue but an important issue involving cultural adaptation and market strategy. Through this study, we aim to provide valuable insights for translation practitioners, brand managers, and cross-cultural communication researchers and contribute to the international dissemination of Chinese culture. This article argues that CHAGEE's successful expansion in the international market is largely due to its balanced use of domestication and foreignization translation strategies, effectively bridging cultural differences while preserving the brand's Chinese tea culture heritage.

# Overview

Consumer demand for transparency pushed advertising and product information from vague persuasion toward standardized, verifiable terminology and formats—what we can call “technical English.” This shift entailed precise claim vocabularies, test-based language, controlled label formats, and disclosure templates that enabled consumers and regulators to audit what was being sold and how. The arc runs from 19th-century consumer activism and early self-regulation through early-20th-century statutory reforms, to mid-20th-century agency rulemaking that codified technical terminology in labeling and advertising, with ongoing refinements in the late 20th and 21st centuries as consumers demanded clearer, comparable, and legally defensible information across markets. <cite id="ca4bb7f0-0">Modern consumers evaluate, compare, and question marketing information, and they increasingly treat transparency as a signal of ethical conduct and accountability, so firms that fail face reputational and purchase-intent penalties</cite>.

# Industrial-era consumer activism and early self-regulation (19th–early 20th century)

Public skepticism of exaggerated or unverifiable claims created an early market for “truth in advertising,” prompting local movements, industry coalitions, and state laws that required specific, measurable language in commercial copy. <cite id="c2a74487-3">From the 1850s through the early 20th century, advertisers faced stereotypes as “shady operators” and recognized that outlandish patent-remedy and manipulative copy bred public skepticism that weakened persuasive effectiveness; in response, managers organized vigilance committees, lobbied for state laws making false advertising a crime, educated consumers with pamphlets and audits, and surveilled ads to verify promised performance</cite>. These efforts established routines of concrete proof, measurable outcomes, and explicit disclaimers—hallmarks of technical English—because consumers and watchdogs demanded claims that could be checked against evidence.

The Procter & Gamble case illustrates the stakes. <cite id="c2a74487-3">P&G repeatedly faced penalties for unverifiable technical-sounding claims like “removal of 99% bacteria” and for provocative pop-science analogies that obscured evidence requirements; regulators’ fines and public backlash forced the company to learn “the hard way” that marketing must respect laws, public order, and “moral and legal bottom lines,” reinforcing the need for evidence-based, transparent language</cite>. As markets grew national, the convergence of activism and legal reforms moved advertising away from emotive manipulation toward precise, testable terminology and explicit performance claims.

# Statutory reforms and the codification of technical terminology (early 20th–mid 20th century)

Federal consumer protection laws institutionalized the demand for transparency by mandating standardized claim vocabularies, test-based language, and labeling templates. <cite id="15bd296c-1">In the United States, the FDA and FTC jointly regulate food advertising: the FDA polices labeling and nutrition claims, while the FTC targets deceptive tactics, with the FTC Act (Sec. 5) preventing deceptive or unfair practices to enhance informed choice</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-2">Regulatory authority directly governs express claims in ads, reflecting a shift from rhetorical manipulation to precise, verifiable language; agencies empowered to police “psychological” persuasion formalized the expectation that advertisers substantiate technical-sounding claims</cite>. 

These mandates produced standardized English for what could be sold and how it must be described. <cite id="15bd296c-3">For dietary supplements, the FTC regulates claims in all media, while the FDA governs claims on labeling and packaging; the agencies’ shared jurisdiction around “facts” panels and substantiation norms forced consistent, technical terminology across ad and shelf</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-0">During crises (e.g., lockdowns), temporary relaxations of labeling requirements were explicitly noted, underscoring that standardized labels and nutritional disclosure are core to consumer protection and choice</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-4">Globally, frameworks like the EU’s General Food Law (Regulation 178/2002) center traceability, transparency, and prohibition of false health claims, embedding technical vocabulary and process standards into marketing ecosystems</cite>.

# Case studies: how transparency demands shaped technical English

- Standardized geographic/place terminology in wine markets. <cite id="77646bf6-0">From the 1980s, the U.S. wine industry developed a standardized system of American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) that provided collective labeling options; AVA labeling became a key element of product differentiation and complemented brand strategies</cite>. By fixing place-based descriptors into technical geographic terms, consumers could audit origin and style, turning qualitative descriptors into legible, comparable labels.

- Test-based pesticide and household-chemical labeling. <cite id="15bd296c-1">Regulatory regimes for foods and supplements required specific, measurable claims and standard formats; agencies jointly enforced truth-in-advertising and label accuracy to prevent misleading efficacy or safety language</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-3">Shared jurisdiction over claims on labels and in ads produced consistent “facts” panels and standardized terminology across media, reinforcing technical English as the baseline</cite>. 

- Front-of-pack labels and “plain vs. technical” English. <cite id="77646bf6-1">Research shows consumers prefer simplified front-of-pack formats like the Multiple Traffic Light (MTL), which uses technical terms that are nonetheless more comprehensible and accepted across socioeconomic levels; simpler formats reduce decision time and increase identification of healthier products</cite>. At the same time, more complex systems (e.g., Rating Stars, GDAs) often underperform, suggesting that “technical English” must be simplified and standardized to be trustworthy. <cite id="77646bf6-1">Formative research and social marketing are then used to translate technical criteria into accessible visuals and text, coupling standardization with communication to build trust</cite>.

- Corporate disclosure norms and AI-generated content. <cite id="ca4bb7f0-2">As generative AI embeds into advertising, disclosure that content was AI-assisted has become a critical transparency cue; studies find mixed effects on trust, revealing that explicit, standardized disclosure language can strengthen or weaken credibility depending on context, which pressures marketers to adopt precise, verifiable disclosure templates</cite>. This mirrors earlier transparency norms: explicit, standardized English for what was used and how, to enable persuasion knowledge processes.

- Sectoral standardization: denominations and classification schemes. <cite id="77646bf6-0">AVAs exemplify how consumer demand for legible provenance and differentiation drove technical classification vocabulary that travels across markets as part of marketing strategy</cite>. Similar standardization appears in safety and sustainability classifications, where consumers’ need to compare products pushes vendors and regulators to adopt shared technical terminology.

# Ongoing consumer battles and contested technical terms (late 20th–21st century)

Transparency demands continue to shape technical English as consumers contest ambiguous terms and push for verifiable standards. <cite id="15bd296c-4">Misleading environmental and health claims draw sustained consumer and regulatory scrutiny; high-profile backlashes (e.g., Nike, Coca-Cola) prompt adoption of stricter standards and clearer language</cite>. <cite id="77646bf6-1">When labels use technical terms consumers don’t understand (e.g., complex GDAs) or map onto the wrong mental models (e.g., rating stars conflated with quality ratings), trust erodes; agencies and industry then refine terminology and communication to restore comprehension</cite>. 

Regulatory enforcement also polices the line between technical accuracy and manipulative precision. <cite id="c2a74487-3">The FTC’s Sec. 5 authority treats deceptive or unfair application of “psychological” science as unlawful, reinforcing that jargon without evidence is not protected speech</cite>. <cite id="ca4bb7f0-0">Because modern consumers actively compare and question claims, firms face reputational and purchase-intent penalties for opacity; transparency cues in advertising build trust and brand image</cite>. These dynamics keep technical English precise, bounded by evidence, and legible to consumers.

# Mechanisms: Why transparency drives technicalization

Three mechanisms link consumer demand to technical English. First, comprehension and choice: <cite id="15bd296c-1">standardized claim vocabularies and label formats by FDA/FTC improve comparability and informed choice</cite>; <cite id="77646bf6-1">simpler, technical front-of-pack formats raise understanding and reduce decision time</cite>. Second, liability and legitimacy: <cite id="c2a74487-3">early BBB efforts and state laws made false advertising a crime and institutionalized auditing of claims, forcing precise, verifiable language</cite>; <cite id="ca4bb7f0-2">AI disclosure experiments show that explicit, standardized transparency cues can change perceived credibility, incentivizing technical disclosure practices</cite>. Third, market coherence: <cite id="77646bf6-0">industry-wide technical terminology (e.g., AVAs) becomes part of marketing strategy precisely because consumers demand legible provenance and differentiation</cite>; <cite id="15bd296c-3">shared jurisdiction over claims on shelf and in ads compels consistent “facts” panels and terminology</cite>.

# Trade-offs and tensions

The push for transparency has not eliminated ambiguity; it has rechanneled it into controlled vocabularies and formats. <cite id="77646bf6-1">Technical terms can be comprehensible or not, and formats that fail consumer comprehension invite mistrust rather than empowerment</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-4">Consumer activism and regulatory enforcement have largely curtailed misleading sustainability and health claims, but companies still face backlashes when technical or metaphorical language confuses or misleads</cite>. <cite id="c2a74487-3">Moreover, early self-regulation sought respectability and social standing, revealing that transparency reforms often reflect both consumer demand and the industry’s desire to legitimize itself</cite>.

# Synthesis

Consumer demand for transparency catalyzed a historic shift from emotive, rhetorical advertising to standardized, evidence-based English in marketing. Activist and BBB-era pressures, statutory reforms (FDA/FTC, EU GFL), and sectoral rules created precise claim vocabularies, test-based language, and legible label formats that consumers could audit. Case studies from wine AVAs, pesticide/supplement labeling, and front-of-pack design show how contested terms were codified into shared technical conventions to restore trust and comparability. Today, transparency continues to refine “technical English,” as AI disclosure and sustainability claims reveal that precise, verifiable language is both a technical and rhetorical necessity in a digitally connected marketplace. <cite id="c2a74487-3">The arc from vigilance committees and state laws to modern agency oversight demonstrates that when consumers demand transparency, markets and regulators respond by making English in marketing more technical, standardized, and accountable</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-1">Truth-in-advertising frameworks in the U.S. and the EU’s General Food Law institutionalize this shift, centering traceability, transparency, and verifiable claims</cite>. <cite id="77646bf6-1">Where technical terminology fails the comprehension test, reform cycles reinvent it—e.g., simplifying front-of-pack labels while preserving their technical rigor</cite>. <cite id="ca4bb7f0-0">Ultimately, transparency is not merely informative—it shapes brand fairness perceptions and image, reinforcing why “technical English” in marketing is both a legal compliance strategy and a trust-building technology</cite>.

Snippet: The American Truth-in-Advertising movement represented, in part, a collective search for respectability and social standing. From the 1850s into the early twentieth century, advertising agencies, newspapers, and magazines had depended on patent medicine advertisements for a significant share of income, and those ads notoriously made outlandish claims of miraculous impacts (Young, 1961). Even when advertising agencies attracted business from a wider set of products, their advertisements often embraced manipulative or deceptive tactics. As a result, advertising executives confronted negative stereotypes that depicted them as shady operators who lacked scruples. At the same time, some upscale marketers concluded that the prevalence of misleading claims in advertising copy had generated widespread public skepticism about advertising in general, reducing its capacity to move consumers to buy. 4 For a cluster of advertising managers in more established agencies and corporate managers responsible for marketing, these concerns justified collective action to rein in the worst kinds of duplicity in the American marketplace. 

The first efforts took place within Midwestern cities, beginning in Minneapolis, and then spread to urban centers around the country. In addition to organizing local "vigilance committees" devoted to an ideology of truthfulness in commercial speech, early leaders lobbied for new state laws that made false advertising a criminal misdemeanor. The biggest focus of these new urban organizations was on retail marketing practices. But in New York City, Boston, and other large eastern cities, the BBB (as they came to be called by the early 1920s) also targeted sales of unlisted securities (that is, investment vehicles not listed on one of the country's established stock exchanges). 5 rom the outset, the most important strategy of the BBBs was to educate consumers and investors so that they could sidestep bad deals and outright scams. The Bureaus churned out educational pamphlets, deputized spokespersons to speak to community organizations and write articles for city newspapers, and placed cautionary ads all over urban America. Alongside this strategy of pre-vention, BBBs established mechanisms to monitor marketing practices. Every BBB encouraged local residents to bring it complaints of unfair or unscrupulous sales tactics, and also surveyed local ads, and then sent out employees to see whether businesses lived up to their advertised promises. If a Bureau found evidence of deceptive selling, it would contact the business in question to seek redress.

# Overview

Consumer demand for transparency pushed advertising and product information from vague persuasion toward standardized, verifiable terminology and formats—what we can call “technical English.” This shift entailed precise claim vocabularies, test-based language, controlled label formats, and disclosure templates that enabled consumers and regulators to audit what was being sold and how. The arc runs from 19th-century consumer activism and early self-regulation through early-20th-century statutory reforms, to mid-20th-century agency rulemaking that codified technical terminology in labeling and advertising, with ongoing refinements in the late 20th and 21st centuries as consumers demanded clearer, comparable, and legally defensible information across markets. <cite id="ca4bb7f0-0">Modern consumers evaluate, compare, and question marketing information, and they increasingly treat transparency as a signal of ethical conduct and accountability, so firms that fail face reputational and purchase-intent penalties</cite>.

# Industrial-era consumer activism and early self-regulation (19th–early 20th century)

Public skepticism of exaggerated or unverifiable claims created an early market for “truth in advertising,” prompting local movements, industry coalitions, and state laws that required specific, measurable language in commercial copy. <cite id="c2a74487-3">From the 1850s through the early 20th century, advertisers faced stereotypes as “shady operators” and recognized that outlandish patent-remedy and manipulative copy bred public skepticism that weakened persuasive effectiveness; in response, managers organized vigilance committees, lobbied for state laws making false advertising a crime, educated consumers with pamphlets and audits, and surveilled ads to verify promised performance</cite>. These efforts established routines of concrete proof, measurable outcomes, and explicit disclaimers—hallmarks of technical English—because consumers and watchdogs demanded claims that could be checked against evidence.

The Procter & Gamble case illustrates the stakes. <cite id="c2a74487-3">P&G repeatedly faced penalties for unverifiable technical-sounding claims like “removal of 99% bacteria” and for provocative pop-science analogies that obscured evidence requirements; regulators’ fines and public backlash forced the company to learn “the hard way” that marketing must respect laws, public order, and “moral and legal bottom lines,” reinforcing the need for evidence-based, transparent language</cite>. As markets grew national, the convergence of activism and legal reforms moved advertising away from emotive manipulation toward precise, testable terminology and explicit performance claims.

# Statutory reforms and the codification of technical terminology (early 20th–mid 20th century)

Federal consumer protection laws institutionalized the demand for transparency by mandating standardized claim vocabularies, test-based language, and labeling templates. <cite id="15bd296c-1">In the United States, the FDA and FTC jointly regulate food advertising: the FDA polices labeling and nutrition claims, while the FTC targets deceptive tactics, with the FTC Act (Sec. 5) preventing deceptive or unfair practices to enhance informed choice</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-2">Regulatory authority directly governs express claims in ads, reflecting a shift from rhetorical manipulation to precise, verifiable language; agencies empowered to police “psychological” persuasion formalized the expectation that advertisers substantiate technical-sounding claims</cite>. 

These mandates produced standardized English for what could be sold and how it must be described. <cite id="15bd296c-3">For dietary supplements, the FTC regulates claims in all media, while the FDA governs claims on labeling and packaging; the agencies’ shared jurisdiction around “facts” panels and substantiation norms forced consistent, technical terminology across ad and shelf</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-0">During crises (e.g., lockdowns), temporary relaxations of labeling requirements were explicitly noted, underscoring that standardized labels and nutritional disclosure are core to consumer protection and choice</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-4">Globally, frameworks like the EU’s General Food Law (Regulation 178/2002) center traceability, transparency, and prohibition of false health claims, embedding technical vocabulary and process standards into marketing ecosystems</cite>.

# Case studies: how transparency demands shaped technical English

- Standardized geographic/place terminology in wine markets. <cite id="77646bf6-0">From the 1980s, the U.S. wine industry developed a standardized system of American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) that provided collective labeling options; AVA labeling became a key element of product differentiation and complemented brand strategies</cite>. By fixing place-based descriptors into technical geographic terms, consumers could audit origin and style, turning qualitative descriptors into legible, comparable labels.

- Test-based pesticide and household-chemical labeling. <cite id="15bd296c-1">Regulatory regimes for foods and supplements required specific, measurable claims and standard formats; agencies jointly enforced truth-in-advertising and label accuracy to prevent misleading efficacy or safety language</cite>. <cite id="15bd296c-3">Shared jurisdiction over claims on labels and in ads produced consistent “facts” panels and standardized terminology across media, reinforcing technical English as the baseline</cite>. 

- Front-of-pack labels and “plain vs. technical” English. <cite id="77646bf6-1">Research shows consumers prefer simplified front-of-pack formats like the Multiple Traffic Light (MTL), which uses technical terms that are nonetheless more comprehensible and accepted across socioeconomic levels; simpler formats reduce decision time and increase identification of healthier products</cite>. At the same time, more complex systems (e.g., Rating Stars, GDAs) often underperform, suggesting that “technical English” must be simplified and standardized to be trustworthy. <cite id="77646bf6-1">Formative research and social marketing are then used to translate technical criteria into accessible visuals and text, coupling standardization with communication to build trust</cite>.

- Corporate disclosure norms and AI-generated content. <cite id="ca4bb7f0-2">As generative AI embeds into advertising, disclosure that content was AI-assisted has become a critical transparency cue; studies find mixed effects on trust, revealing that explicit, standardized disclosure language can strengthen or weaken credibility depending on context, which pressures marketers to adopt precise, verifiable disclosure templates</cite>. This mirrors earlier transparency norms: explicit, standardized English for what was used and how, to enable persuasion knowledge processes.

- Sectoral standardization: denominations and classification schemes. <cite id="77646bf6-0">AVAs exemplify how consumer demand for legible provenance and differentiation drove technical classification vocabulary that travels across markets as part of marketing strategy</cite>. Similar standardization appears in safety and sustainability classifications, where consumers’ need to compare products pushes vendors and regulators to adopt shared technical terminology.

# Ongoing consumer battles and contested technical terms (late 20th–21st century)

Transparency demands continue to shape technical English as consumers contest ambiguous terms and push for verifiable standards. <cite id="15bd296c-4">Misleading environmental and health claims draw sustained consumer and regulatory scrutiny; high-profile backlashes (e.g., Nike, Coca-Cola) prompt adoption of stricter standards and clearer language</cite>. <cite id="77646bf6-1">When labels use technical terms consumers don’t understand (e.g., complex GDAs) or map onto the wrong mental models (e.g., rating stars conflated with quality ratings), trust erodes; agencies and industry then refine terminology and communication to restore comprehension</cite>. 

Regulatory enforcement also polices the line between technical accuracy and manipulative precision. <cite id="c2a74487-3">The FTC’s Sec. 5 authority treats deceptive or unfair application of “psychological” science as unlawful, reinforcing that jargon without evidence is not protected speech</cite>. <cite id="ca4bb7f0-0">Because modern consumers actively compare and question claims, firms face reputational and purchase-intent penalties for opacity; transparency cues in advertising build trust and brand image</cite>. These dynamics keep technical English precise, bounded by evidence, and legible to consumers.

# Mechanisms: Why transparency drives technicalization

Three mechanisms link consumer demand to technical English. Title: From AI disclosure to purchase intention: The mediating role of trust and the moderating effect of collectivistic orientation in Vietnam
Snippet: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has fundamentally transformed advertising practices, enabling automated content generation, predictive targeting, and large-scale personalization of marketing communication (Davenport et al., 2020). As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in brand communication processes, the disclosure that advertising content was created or assisted by AI has emerged as a critical transparency issue for marketers and regulators. While transparency is traditionally associated with improved credibility and ethical communication, emerging research suggests that the effects of AI disclosure are more complex and may vary depending on psychological, contextual, and cultural factors (Campbell et al., 2021;Baek et al., 2024). 

Consumer trust represents a central concern in this context. Trust plays a pivotal role in reducing perceived risk and uncertainty in mar-keting relationships, thereby shaping behavioral outcomes such as purchase intention (Morgan & Hunt, 1994;Mayer et al., 1995). Prior research indicates that transparency cues in advertising, including disclosure of sponsorship or data usage, can influence consumer trust and persuasion outcomes through the activation of persuasion knowledge processes (Friestad & Wright, 1994). However, recent studies on AI-generated advertising reveal mixed findings, showing that disclosure may either enhance trust by signaling honesty or weaken credibility by highlighting the artificial nature of the content (Baek et al., 2024;Kietzmann et al., 2021). These inconsistent results suggest the need to examine the psychological mechanisms through which AI disclosure influences consumer responses. 

Cultural context may further shape how transparency signals are interpreted. In collectivistic societies, where interpersonal trust, social harmony, and relational authenticity are emphasized, consumers may respond differently to automated advertising compared with consumers in individualistic markets (Hofstede, 2011;Nguyen-Thu, 2018). Despite the growing literature on AI-driven marketing communication, empirical evidence examining the trust mechanism linking AI disclosure to behavioral outcomes in collectivistic emerging markets remains limited. Addressing this gap is particularly important in rapidly digitizing economies such as Vietnam, where AI adoption in marketing communication is accelerating alongside strong collectivistic cultural values.

Title: American Better Business Bureaus, the Truth-in-Advertising Movement, and the Complexities of Legitimizing Business Self-Regulation over the Long Term
Snippet: The American Truth-in-Advertising movement represented, in part, a collective search for respectability and social standing. From the 1850s into the early twentieth century, advertising agencies, newspapers, and magazines had depended on patent medicine advertisements for a significant share of income, and those ads notoriously made outlandish claims of miraculous impacts (Young, 1961). Even when advertising agencies attracted business from a wider set of products, their advertisements often embraced manipulative or deceptive tactics. As a result, advertising executives confronted negative stereotypes that depicted them as shady operators who lacked scruples. At the same time, some upscale marketers concluded that the prevalence of misleading claims in advertising copy had generated widespread public skepticism about advertising in general, reducing its capacity to move consumers to buy. 4 For a cluster of advertising managers in more established agencies and corporate managers responsible for marketing, these concerns justified collective action to rein in the worst kinds of duplicity in the American marketplace. 

The first efforts took place within Midwestern cities, beginning in Minneapolis, and then spread to urban centers around the country. In addition to organizing local "vigilance committees" devoted to an ideology of truthfulness in commercial speech, early leaders lobbied for new state laws that made false advertising a criminal misdemeanor. The biggest focus of these new urban organizations was on retail marketing practices. But in New York City, Boston, and other large eastern cities, the BBB (as they came to be called by the early 1920s) also targeted sales of unlisted securities (that is, investment vehicles not listed on one of the country's established stock exchanges). 5 rom the outset, the most important strategy of the BBBs was to educate consumers and investors so that they could sidestep bad deals and outright scams. The Bureaus churned out educational pamphlets, deputized spokespersons to speak to community organizations and write articles for city newspapers, and placed cautionary ads all over urban America. Alongside this strategy of pre-vention, BBBs established mechanisms to monitor marketing practices. Every BBB encouraged local residents to bring it complaints of unfair or unscrupulous sales tactics, and also surveyed local ads, and then sent out employees to see whether businesses lived up to their advertised promises. If a Bureau found evidence of deceptive selling, it would contact the business in question to seek redress.

documents.snippet:
The American Truth-in-Advertising movement represented, in part, a collective search for respectability and social standing. From the 1850s into the early twentieth century, advertising agencies, newspapers, and magazines had depended on patent medicine advertisements for a significant share of income, and those ads notoriously made outlandish claims of miraculous impacts (Young, 1961). Even when advertising agencies attracted business from a wider set of products, their advertisements often embraced manipulative or deceptive tactics. As a result, advertising executives confronted negative stereotypes that depicted them as shady operators who lacked scruples. At the same time, some upscale marketers concluded that the prevalence of misleading claims in advertising copy had generated widespread public skepticism about advertising in general, reducing its capacity to move consumers to buy. 4 For a cluster of advertising managers in more established agencies and corporate managers responsible for marketing, these concerns justified collective action to rein in the worst kinds of duplicity in the American marketplace. 

The first efforts took place within Midwestern cities, beginning in Minneapolis, and then spread to urban centers around the country. In addition to organizing local "vigilance committees" devoted to an ideology of truthfulness in commercial speech, early leaders lobbied for new state laws that made false advertising a criminal misdemeanor. The biggest focus of these new urban organizations was on retail marketing practices. But in New York City, Boston, and other large eastern cities, the BBB (as they came to be called by the early 1920s) also targeted sales of unlisted securities (that is, investment vehicles not listed on one of the country's established stock exchanges). 5 rom the outset, the most important strategy of the BBBs was to educate consumers and investors so that they could sidestep bad deals and outright scams. The Bureaus churned out educational pamphlets, deputized spokespersons to speak to community organizations and write articles for city newspapers, and placed cautionary ads all over urban America. Alongside this strategy of pre-vention, BBBs established mechanisms to monitor marketing practices. Every BBB encouraged local residents to bring it complaints of unfair or unscrupulous sales tactics, and also surveyed local ads, and then sent out employees to see whether businesses lived up to their advertised promises. If a Bureau found evidence of deceptive selling, it would contact the business in question to seek redress.

Title: The Influence of Adaptation and Standardization of the Marketing Mix on Performance: a Meta-Analysis
Snippet: Nowadays standardization studies comprise all elements of the marketing mixproduct, promotion, price and distribution (Özsomer & Simonin, 2004;Vrontis & Kitchen, 2005), although promotion and product have received more attention (e.g. Baalbaki & Malhotra, 1993;Kotler, 1986;Laroche, Kirpalani, Pons, & Zhou, 2001;Levitt, 1983;Papavassiliou & Stathakopoulos, 1997;Samiee & Roth, 1992).

The former is concerned with the philosophy, principles, and technology used in planning and implementing marketing decisions. The latterthe purpose of this studyrefers to the elements of the marketing mix. 

Despite some studies that have analyzed the standardization concept (e.g. Jain, 1989;Özsomer, Bodur, & Cavusgil, 1991), its consensual understanding has yet to be established (Ryans, Griffith, & White, 2003). Standardization is the use of the same marketing program in different countries or regions, regarding the product offered, the promotion employed, the price established and the distribution process chosen (Elinder, 1965;Jain, 1989Jain, , 2007;;Levitt, 1983;Özsomer & Simonin, 2004;Roostal, 1963;Sands, 1979;Szymanski, Bharadwaj, & Varadara, 1993;Viswanathan & Dickson 2007). 

The main argument supporting the standardization strategy is the belief that the world is becoming more and more homogeneous, especially as a result of the advances in communication and technology (Jain, 1989;Levitt, 1983). As a consequence, tastes and cultures are becoming homogeneous; world consumers are sharing preferences, needs, desires and demands (Jain, 1989(Jain, , 2007;;Levitt, 1983;Vrontis & Papasolomou, 2005). This similarity of demands, along with convergent cultures and the lowering of barriers, would make it possible for companies to sell more standardized products, with standardized marketing programs (Zou & Cavusgil 2002). 

Standardization, thus, allows focus on common segments, bringing economy of scale and more consistent promotions.
